newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts seek update on savings from Axa-UAP merge.
newsitem.headline: Analysts seek update on savings from Axa-UAP merge.

text.p: Financial analysts are hoping for a progress report on the mega-merger of French insurers Axa SA and UAP when the two companies announce their 1996 results on Wednesday.
"We'd like to see updated estimates on cost savings -- how likely they are to hit targets," Brian Shea of Salomon Brothers said.

Axa and UAP are integrating their operations after announcing last November a share swap creating the world's second largest insurer and will release separate sets of figures on Wednesday for the last time. As of 1997, their accounts will be consolidated.

Analysts expect robust 1996 operating earnings for Axa and UAP, France's largest insurer. But provisions to prevent UAP's lossmaking operations weighing on the new group's future are expected to plunge UAP into a big bottom line loss.

Axa, which has enjoyed a reputation as the best quality French insurance player, had 1995 profits of 2.73 billion francs. It said last month it was "at ease" with analysts' forecasts of 1996 net attributable profit of 3.6.-3.9 billion francs.

This would represent earnings per share growth of 18 to 28 percent. While most analysts see profit of around 3.7-3.8 billion, some do not rule out chances it could be four billion francs or slightly higher. The performance will be helped by strong results from Australian life insurer National Mutual and The Equitable of the United States.
Its nonlife and reinsurance operations are believed to have had a strong second half and its holding operations are expected to swing to profit after a loss of 248 million francs in 1995.
But UAP's accounts are expected to undergo a "once and for all" clean up, pushing it into loss for second year in a row.
Press reports have said UAP, privatised in 1994 and seen as more stodgy and bureaucratic in style than aggressive, fast-growing Axa, will post a six-to-seven billion franc 1996 loss after provisions.

"A purge of UAP's acounts which would be translated by a loss of six billions would be...appreciated by the market," said Jean-Baptiste Bellon of Deutsche Bank. UAP had a loss of 2.1 billion after heavy provisions in 1995.

The new provisions are expected to deal with restructuring, property, insurance and banking problems. The charges are expected to include 400 million francs to end lossmaking by UAP's banking arm, Banque Worms, and other charges to restore the finances of its life and group insurance operations.

There are also expected to be writedowns of the carrying value of UAP's holdings in BNP and Suez, in its balance sheet at greater than market value. "What will be of great interest is how much of UAP is written off -- what is the net asset value of UAP and of Axa itself," said one analyst.
One analyst said the writedown could knock six percent of UAP's net asset value and "an accurate estimate of post acquisition adjusted net asset value could still be elusive."
But analysts are looking for operating earnings for UAP of 1.71 billion francs in 1995, helped by strong non-life results, particularly in France and Germany.
Axa has said the merger should allow 1997 savings of about 200 million francs and analysts say the most optimistic scenario calls for costs savings of 2.1 billion francs by 1999.

But some analysts are not convinced that the merger, described by many as more of a takeover by Axa, was the best use of Axa's capital. Shea said he did not believe the transaction would "meaningfully improve Axa's ROE profile."

"Moreover, the 'old Axa' was more plugged into exciting high-growth operations," he said in an investors' note, noting the weighting of the group's premium income generated by its most "exciting franchises", The Equitable and National Mutual, will fall by more than half to 32 percent from 15 percent.
